title: The Internet’s undersea backbone is slipping into the danger zone
gist: In an interview about her book Undersea War, Elisabeth Braw argues subsea cable security is deteriorating as treaty norms erode, citing suspicious anchor-dragging incidents and Iran's cable toll threat in Hormuz. She notes private ownership of critical infrastructure means operators' commercial incentives diverge from governments' redundancy needs.

insights.claim: About 60 percent of undersea cable damage is due to human error in fishing and shipping and 150 to 200 cables are damaged annually, usually repaired quickly, which gives a baseline against suspected sabotage.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: The baseline means most cuts are noise, so attribution is hard.

insights.claim: In the Christmas Day 2024 incident, the Russian-linked tanker Eagle S dragged its anchor about 90 km, damaging four data cables and the Estlink 2 power cable; Finland tried to prosecute three officers, while the Chinese ship Yi Peng 3's crew was not prosecuted.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Prosecution treatment varies by flag state, a signal of the attribution and legal gray zone.
insights.locator: One of the more notorious incidents

insights.claim: Taiwan convicted the captain of the Chinese-owned Hong Tai for cutting a cable and sentenced him to three years in June 2025, and later raised penalties to up to seven years.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Legal deterrence is rising in exposed jurisdictions.
insights.locator: On the other side of the world

insights.claim: Braw says experienced merchant vessels suddenly became sloppy and dragged anchors across several regions, which she calls extremely suspicious although motives may never be known.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Patterns across Baltic, Norway and Taiwan waters suggest gray-zone tactics, insurers and operators price this risk.
insights.locator: The fascinating thing about subsea cables

insights.claim: Braw also flags Russian and Chinese research vessels loitering near cables, with China not notifying coastal states of research, alongside expanding submarine fleets and undersea drones; a UK/Norway/US operation confronted Russian submarines practicing disabling cables near Svalbard.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Capability development, not only anchors, expands the threat to cables.
insights.locator: But then we have what you just brought up

themes.theme: Erosion of rules-based order and Hormuz tolls

insights.claim: Braw argues cable security relied on near-universal treaty adherence (UNCLOS adopted in 1982) and is now fraying as key countries commit less, while cables have become far more economically critical than Cold War telephone lines.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Greater dependence plus weaker norms raises tail risk for financial hubs reliant on subsea links.
insights.locator: Exactly. It worked for so long

insights.claim: Iran claimed it was no longer bound by UNCLOS and said it would charge tolls on Strait of Hormuz cables, which Braw says violates UNCLOS and raises the question of whether other states will copy it.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Toll precedent could add costs for cable operators and spread to other chokepoints.

insights.claim: Three cable projects planned in the Gulf region were suspended or abandoned with force majeure after the war began in February, because stationary installation ships would be 'sitting ducks'; one third of India's westbound digital connectivity goes through the Persian Gulf.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: War delays new capacity and leaves routes concentrated, raising the value of alternatives.

insights.claim: Virtually all cables are now privately owned by consortia and hyperscalers are building their own, yet governments consider them critical infrastructure, and operators will not add redundancy beyond what commercial calculations justify.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Underinvestment in redundancy is likely without subsidies, creating a gap that public money or defense spending may fill.
insights.quote: Companies will look at figures and the hard facts

insights.claim: Braw says governments don't have the money to create backups for every cable and the only alternative is subsidizing new cables, as with Taiwan's Matsu Islands.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Subsidy-backed resilience is selective, so expect targeted state funding for strategic routes.

insights.claim: Cable installation and repair crews are at the front line of the clash between geopolitics and modern economies, since they must operate near projectiles and weapons.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Repair capacity could be a bottleneck in wartime, lengthening outages.
